title: Evolution and Ecosystems: Natural Selection, Food Webs, Energy Flow, and Cycles
objectives: Students will explain natural selection using its four conditions (variation, inheritance, overproduction, selection) and use population data to describe how a trait becomes more common over generations.
Students will identify and evaluate evidence for evolution, including fossils, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, and DNA and protein comparisons.
Students will classify organisms in food chains and food webs as producers, consumers (primary, secondary, tertiary), or decomposers and predict the effects of a change in one population.
Students will use the 10% rule to calculate the energy available at each level of an energy pyramid and calculate the actual percentage of energy transferred between levels.
Students will describe the main processes of the carbon and nitrogen cycles and interpret data about them.
teach:
Week 6 Science: Evolution and Ecosystems

Objectives

  • Explain natural selection using its four conditions and use population data to describe how a trait becomes more common over generations.
  • Identify evidence for evolution: fossils, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, and DNA and protein comparisons.
  • Classify organisms in food chains and food webs and predict what happens when one population changes.
  • Use the 10% rule to calculate energy at each level of an energy pyramid, and calculate actual transfer percentages from data.
  • Describe the main processes of the carbon and nitrogen cycles and interpret data about them.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in three colors (green for producers, blue for consumers, brown for decomposers).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Calculators (the GED Science test provides an on-screen calculator).
  • Index cards, one per student, for the memory card “Very Interesting Organisms Survive” and the 10% rule.
  • This week's 12 practice items on the course page for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Three quick questions: why pesticides stop working, where your lunch got its energy, and what happens to a dead leaf.
Direct instruction20Natural selection and adaptation; evidence for evolution; food chains and webs; energy pyramids and the 10% rule; carbon and nitrogen cycles. Worked Examples 1–3.
Guided practice15Seed-eating birds after a drought, a pond energy pyramid, and a cycles check, with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these three questions on the board and give students two minutes to jot answers.

  1. A farmer sprays the same insect poison on a field every year. After about five years, the poison barely works. Why?
  2. Think of what you ate for lunch. Trace its energy back as far as you can.
  3. A leaf falls to the forest floor in autumn. Where does the carbon in that leaf end up?

Answers:

  1. A few insects in the original population happened to be resistant to the poison. They survived the spraying and reproduced, passing resistance to their offspring. Each year a larger share of the population was resistant. The insects did not “get used to” the poison; the population changed because resistant insects survived. (This is natural selection, today's first big idea.)
  2. Example: a chicken sandwich. The chicken ate corn; the corn got its energy from sunlight through photosynthesis. Every food chain on land starts with the sun and a producer.
  3. Decomposers (fungi and bacteria) break the leaf down. Their cellular respiration releases much of the carbon into the air as carbon dioxide, and some stays in the soil. Plants later take that carbon dioxide back in. Matter cycles.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Evolution and natural selection (6 minutes). Evolution is change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations. The main way it happens is natural selection, which needs four conditions. Have students write the memory sentence on an index card:

Very Interesting Organisms Survive

  • Variation: individuals in a population differ in their traits (color, size, beak shape, resistance).
  • Inheritance: many of those traits are passed from parents to offspring through genes.
  • Overproduction: organisms produce more offspring than can survive, so they compete for food, mates, and space.
  • Selection: individuals with traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, so their traits become more common in the next generation.

Stress three points that the GED tests again and again:

  • Populations evolve; individuals do not. A single lizard cannot change its genes during its life. The percentage of lizards with a trait changes from one generation to the next.
  • Acquired traits are not inherited. A weightlifter's large muscles or a dog's clipped tail are not passed on.
  • Variation comes first. Mutations are random. The environment does not create the helpful trait on demand; it only “selects” among traits that already exist.

An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment (camouflage coloring, thick fur in a cold climate, a cactus's waxy skin). Fitness in biology means reproductive success, not strength. The “fittest” individual is the one that leaves the most surviving offspring.

2. Evidence for evolution (3 minutes). Write five headings and one example of each:

  • Fossil record: fossils in deeper (older) rock layers are generally simpler and less like modern species; transitional fossils show in-between forms, such as early whales with small hind legs.
  • Homologous structures: the same bone pattern used for different jobs: a human arm, a bat wing, a whale flipper, a cat leg. Same structure, different function, suggests a common ancestor.
  • Vestigial structures: reduced parts with little or no use today, such as the human tailbone or the tiny hip bones inside some whales.
  • Embryos: early embryos of fish, chickens, and humans look alike (for example, all have tails and pouches in the neck region).
  • DNA and proteins: the fewer differences in DNA or protein sequences, the more closely related two species are, meaning they share a more recent common ancestor.

Contrast homologous with analogous structures: same function, different structure and origin, such as a bird wing and a butterfly wing. Analogous structures do not show close relationship.

3. Food chains and food webs (4 minutes). Draw: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. Label in color:

  • Producers (green) make their own food by photosynthesis: plants, algae.
  • Primary consumers eat producers (herbivores). Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
  • Decomposers (brown) such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and wastes from every level and return nutrients to the soil.

Make a big deal of the arrow: the arrow points to the organism that receives the energy, the eater. Read “grass → grasshopper” as “grass is eaten by the grasshopper.” A food web is many connected food chains. One animal can sit at different levels in different chains: a mouse that eats seeds is a primary consumer, and the same mouse eating a grasshopper is a secondary consumer.

4. Energy pyramids and the 10% rule (4 minutes). Each step in a food chain is a trophic level. Only about 10% of the energy at one level becomes stored in the bodies of the next level. The other 90% is used for life processes (movement, body heat, growth, repair) and lost to the environment as heat, or is never eaten or digested. Draw the pyramid with these numbers:

LevelEnergy (kcal)Step
Producers10,000Start
Primary consumers1,00010,000 × 0.10
Secondary consumers1001,000 × 0.10
Tertiary consumers10100 × 0.10

Two rules for calculations: going up one level, multiply by 0.10 (or move the decimal point one place left); going down one level, multiply by 10. This is why there are far fewer hawks than mice and why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels. Point out: energy flows one way (sun → producers → consumers → heat), but matter cycles.

5. The carbon and nitrogen cycles (3 minutes).

  • Carbon cycle. Removes CO2 from the air: photosynthesis; dissolving into the ocean. Adds CO2 to the air: cellular respiration (by plants, animals, and decomposers), decomposition, burning fuels (combustion), volcanic eruptions. Carbon is stored in living things, soil, ocean water, rocks such as limestone, and fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas formed from ancient organisms). Burning fossil fuels moves carbon that was stored for millions of years into the air quickly.
  • Nitrogen cycle. Air is about 78% nitrogen gas (N2), but plants and animals cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation: bacteria in soil and in root nodules of legumes (beans, peas, clover), plus lightning, convert N2 into ammonia or other usable forms. Nitrification: other bacteria turn ammonia into nitrates. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrates and build proteins and DNA; animals get nitrogen by eating plants. Ammonification: decomposers return nitrogen from dead matter and wastes to the soil as ammonia. Denitrification: bacteria turn nitrates back into N2 gas, which returns to the air.

Stress that bacteria do most of the work in the nitrogen cycle; students often forget this. Quick check: a farmer plants clover one year and corn the next because clover's root bacteria fix nitrogen for the corn.

Worked Example 1 — Natural selection from population data

Scenario: A farmer begins spraying a field with a new pesticide each spring. Each fall, a scientist tests a sample of beetles from the field.

Year12345
Beetles resistant to the pesticide (%)29316888

Question: Describe the trend and explain it using the four conditions of natural selection.

Solution:

  • Trend: the percentage of resistant beetles rose every year, from 2% to 88%. The increase from Year 1 to Year 5 is 88 − 2 = 86 percentage points.
  • Variation: before spraying began, a few beetles (2%) already carried resistance.
  • Inheritance: resistance is genetic, so resistant parents tend to have resistant offspring.
  • Overproduction: beetles lay many more eggs than can survive.
  • Selection: the pesticide killed most non-resistant beetles, so resistant beetles survived and reproduced more. Each generation started with a higher share of resistant beetles.
  • Wrong idea to reject: “The beetles became resistant because they were exposed to the pesticide.” The pesticide did not cause resistance; it selected beetles that already had it.

Worked Example 2 — Energy pyramid calculations, forward and backward

Scenario: The producers in a grassland capture 50,000 kcal per square meter per year. Food chain: grass → mouse → snake → hawk.

(a) How much energy is available to the hawks (tertiary consumers)?

Primary consumers (mice): 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000 kcal
Secondary consumers (snakes): 5,000 × 0.10 = 500 kcal
Tertiary consumers (hawks): 500 × 0.10 = 50 kcal

(b) What percentage of the producers' energy reaches the hawks?

50 ÷ 50,000 = 0.001 = 0.1% (three levels: 0.10 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.001).

(c) Working backward: a different hawk population needs 30 kcal per square meter per year. How much energy must the producers capture?

Snakes: 30 × 10 = 300 kcal. Mice: 300 × 10 = 3,000 kcal. Producers: 3,000 × 10 = 30,000 kcal.

Common error: subtracting 10% at each step (50,000 − 5,000 = 45,000). The rule says 10% is passed on, not 10% lost.

Worked Example 3 — Predicting a change in a food web

Scenario: In a coastal kelp forest, sea urchins eat kelp, and sea otters eat sea urchins. Hunters remove most of the sea otters.

Question: Predict the effect on the sea urchins and on the kelp.

Solution:

  • Write the chain: kelp → sea urchin → sea otter.
  • Step 1: Fewer otters means fewer urchins are eaten, so the urchin population increases.
  • Step 2: More urchins eat more kelp, so the kelp decreases.
  • Key idea: removing a top predator can affect organisms two levels below it. Always follow the arrows one level at a time.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Read each part aloud. Students work in pairs on paper; call on volunteers, then reveal.

Part A. On an island, a population of seed-eating birds was measured before and after a two-year drought. During the drought, small soft seeds became scarce, and most of the remaining seeds were large and hard. Mean beak depth was 9.2 mm before the drought and 9.7 mm in the birds that survived it. Beak depth is strongly inherited.

  1. Which trait changed, and by how much?
  2. Explain the change using the four conditions.
  3. Predict the mean beak depth of chicks hatched after the drought compared with chicks hatched before it.
  4. A student says, “Each bird's beak grew deeper because it had to crack hard seeds.” What is wrong with this statement?

Part B. The producers in a pond capture 8,000 kcal. Food chain: algae → snail → crayfish → raccoon.

  1. How much energy reaches the crayfish?
  2. Which organism is the tertiary consumer, and at which trophic level is it?

Part C.

  1. Name the process that removes carbon dioxide from the air and the process by which decomposers return it.
  2. Which organisms change nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use?

Answers:

  1. Mean beak depth increased from 9.2 mm to 9.7 mm, an increase of 9.7 − 9.2 = 0.5 mm.
  2. Variation: birds differed in beak depth. Inheritance: beak depth is passed on. Overproduction: more birds hatched than the food could support. Selection: during the drought, birds with deeper beaks could crack large hard seeds, so more of them survived to reproduce.
  3. Chicks hatched after the drought should have a deeper mean beak depth than chicks hatched before it, because their parents were mostly the deep-beaked survivors.
  4. It describes an acquired change in individuals. Beaks did not grow deeper from use; birds that already had deeper beaks survived. The population's average changed.
  5. Snail: 8,000 × 0.10 = 800 kcal. Crayfish: 800 × 0.10 = 80 kcal.
  6. The raccoon is the tertiary consumer. It is at the fourth trophic level (algae 1, snail 2, crayfish 3, raccoon 4).
  7. Photosynthesis removes CO2. Decomposers return it through cellular respiration as they break down dead matter (decomposition).
  8. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, in soil and in the root nodules of legumes such as beans and clover. (Lightning also fixes a small amount.)

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–12 on the course page while you circulate. Watch especially for arrow-direction errors on items 6 and 7 and for the subtract-10% error on item 9. Unfinished items become homework.

Checks for Understanding (use during the wrap-up)

  • “What are the four conditions of natural selection?” Expected: variation, inheritance, overproduction, selection (Very Interesting Organisms Survive).
  • “Does an individual evolve?” Expected: No. Populations evolve over generations.
  • “In a food chain, which way does the arrow point?” Expected: toward the eater, the direction energy flows.
  • “Producers have 6,000 kcal. How much reaches secondary consumers?” Expected: 6,000 → 600 → 60 kcal.
  • “Does energy cycle?” Expected: No. Energy flows one way and leaves as heat; matter (carbon, nitrogen) cycles.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

“The animal changed because it needed to.” Students describe evolution as individuals trying or wanting to adapt. Correction: ask, “Did the trait exist before the environment changed?” Then ask, “Which individuals had more babies?” Insist on the words survived, reproduced, and passed on.

Reversing food-chain arrows. Students draw the arrow from the hawk to the snake because “the hawk attacks the snake.” Correction: the arrow follows the energy. Say the chain out loud as “is eaten by.”

Subtracting 10% instead of keeping 10%. Correction: write “× 0.10 going up, × 10 going down” at the top of the scratch paper before any pyramid problem. Sanity check: each level should be one tenth of the level below it, not nine tenths.

Mixing up photosynthesis and respiration in the carbon cycle. Correction: photosynthesis takes in CO2 (plants “breathe in” carbon). Respiration gives off CO2, and plants do both.

Treating “fittest” as “strongest.” Correction: fitness means leaving more surviving offspring. A small, well-camouflaged lizard can be fitter than a big, easily seen one.

Reading too much into DNA data. Students conclude “humans evolved from chimpanzees.” Correction: few differences mean a recent common ancestor, not that one living species turned into another.

Differentiation

Support: Give a frame for natural selection: “Some ____ had ____. That trait helped them ____ in this environment. They had more offspring, who inherited ____. Over generations, ____ became more common.” Give a blank four-row pyramid table for energy problems, and let students keep the memory card out and color-code food chains.

Stretch: Have students calculate actual transfer efficiencies from data (for example, 120 ÷ 1,320 ≈ 9.1%) and explain why real values are not exactly 10%, or explain why clearing and burning a forest raises atmospheric CO2 in two ways (combustion adds it, and fewer trees remain to remove it).

How This Shows Up on the GED

Life science makes up about 40% of the GED Science test, and ecosystems and evolution are frequent topics. Most questions give a stimulus first: a table of population counts over time, a food web drawn as a diagram, an energy pyramid, or a short passage about a cycle. Expect wording like:

  • “Which statement best explains the change in the population shown in the table?”
  • “Based on the food web, which organism is a secondary consumer?”
  • “If the number of [organism] decreased, which change would most likely occur?”
  • “Approximately how much energy is available to the tertiary consumers?”
  • “Which evidence best supports the claim that these species share a common ancestor?”

Formats include multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank (energy at a level, a percentage from a table), drop-down menus completing a statement, drag-and-drop sorting, and hot spots. Teach this routine: (1) read the title and labels, (2) identify the direction of change or of the arrows, (3) calculate if asked, writing each step, (4) choose the answer that explains the data with survival and reproduction, energy flow, or the named cycle process.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above. Preview the exit ticket, the study plan, and this week's Practice GED. Remind students that the on-screen calculator is available for every energy and percentage question.

Evolution and Ecosystems: How Living Things Change and Connect

This lesson covers two connected ideas. First, how populations of living things change over many generations (evolution). Second, how living things are connected by food and by the cycling of matter (ecosystems). On the GED, these topics almost always come with a table, chart, or diagram, so you will practice reading data as you learn.

1. Natural selection

Evolution is a change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations. The main way it happens is natural selection. Natural selection needs four conditions. Remember them with the sentence Very Interesting Organisms Survive:

ConditionWhat it means
VariationIndividuals in a population have different traits.
InheritanceTraits are passed from parents to offspring through genes.
OverproductionMore offspring are born than can survive, so they compete.
SelectionIndividuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.

An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment, such as fur color that matches the surroundings.

Three traps to avoid: (1) Individuals do not evolve; populations do. (2) Traits gained during a lifetime, such as big muscles from lifting weights, are not passed on. (3) The environment does not create a new trait because an animal “needs” it. The helpful trait must already exist in some individuals.

Example 1 — Bacteria and an antibiotic

A patient takes an antibiotic. Most of the bacteria causing the infection die, but a few have a gene that makes them resistant. Those few survive and multiply. Explain what happens to the bacteria population.

Solution: Variation: a few bacteria were already resistant. Inheritance: resistant bacteria pass the gene to their offspring. Overproduction: bacteria multiply very quickly. Selection: the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria, so the resistant ones make up more and more of the population. The antibiotic did not cause resistance; it selected it.

2. Evidence for evolution

  • Fossils: older rock layers hold older fossils. Fossils show how living things changed over time, including in-between (transitional) forms.
  • Homologous structures: the same basic bones used for different jobs, like a human arm, a bat wing, and a whale flipper. This suggests a common ancestor.
  • Vestigial structures: body parts that have little or no use now, like the human tailbone.
  • Embryos: early embryos of many vertebrates look very similar.
  • DNA and proteins: the fewer differences between two species, the more closely related they are.

A bird wing and a butterfly wing do the same job but are built completely differently. These are analogous structures, and they do not show a close relationship. Look for same structure, not same job.

3. Food chains and food webs

Every ecosystem needs energy, and on land almost all of it starts with the sun.

  • Producers (plants, algae) make their own food by photosynthesis.
  • Primary consumers eat producers. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
  • Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead things and wastes and return nutrients to the soil.

In a food chain, the arrow points toward the eater. It shows which way energy moves: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. Read each arrow as “is eaten by.” A food web shows many food chains linked together. The same animal can be at different levels in different chains.

Example 2 — A change in a food web

In a meadow, rabbits eat clover, and foxes eat rabbits. A disease kills most of the foxes. What happens to the rabbits and the clover?

Solution: Follow the arrows one step at a time. Fewer foxes eat rabbits, so rabbits increase. More rabbits eat more clover, so clover decreases.

4. Energy pyramids and the 10% rule

Each step in a food chain is a trophic level. Only about 10% of the energy at one level is passed to the next level. The other 90% is used to move, stay warm, and grow, and it ends up as heat. That is why an energy pyramid is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, and why there are far fewer hawks than mice.

Going up one level: multiply by 0.10 (move the decimal one place left).
Going down one level: multiply by 10.

Example 3 — Using the 10% rule

Producers in a forest capture 20,000 kcal. How much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

Solution:
Primary consumers: 20,000 × 0.10 = 2,000 kcal
Secondary consumers: 2,000 × 0.10 = 200 kcal

Careful: do not subtract 10% (20,000 − 2,000 = 18,000). Only 10% is kept at each step.

Example 4 — Finding the actual percentage from data

A study measured 900 kcal in a level of primary consumers and 72 kcal in the secondary consumers that eat them. What percentage of the energy was passed on?

Solution: 72 ÷ 900 = 0.08. Multiply by 100: 8%. Real ecosystems are close to 10%, but not exactly.

5. The carbon cycle

Energy flows one way, but matter cycles. Carbon moves between the air, living things, oceans, soil, and rocks.

Removes CO2 from the airAdds CO2 to the air
Photosynthesis by plants and algaeCellular respiration by all living things
Ocean water absorbing CO2Decomposition of dead matter
Burning fuels, including fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas)
Volcanic eruptions

6. The nitrogen cycle

Air is about 78% nitrogen gas, but plants and animals cannot use it in that form. Bacteria do most of the work:

  1. Nitrogen fixation: bacteria in soil and in the roots of beans, peas, and clover (and lightning) change nitrogen gas into ammonia.
  2. Nitrification: other bacteria change ammonia into nitrates.
  3. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrates and use them to make proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
  4. Decomposition (ammonification): decomposers return nitrogen from dead things and wastes to the soil as ammonia.
  5. Denitrification: bacteria change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

Try It

1. Producers in a field capture 40,000 kcal. How much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

Show answer

40,000 × 0.10 = 4,000 kcal (primary). 4,000 × 0.10 = 400 kcal (secondary).

2. In the food chain algae → snail → crayfish → raccoon, which organism is the secondary consumer?

Show answer

The crayfish. Algae are producers, the snail is the primary consumer (eats producers), and the crayfish eats the snail.

3. A man builds large muscles by lifting weights for ten years. Will his children be born with large muscles because of his training? Explain.

Show answer

No. Large muscles from training are an acquired trait. They do not change his genes, so they are not inherited.

4. A whale's flipper contains the same arrangement of bones as a human arm. What kind of evidence is this, and what does it suggest?

Show answer

It is a homologous structure. It suggests that whales and humans share a common ancestor.

5. Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air: cellular respiration, burning coal, or photosynthesis?

Show answer

Photosynthesis. Respiration and burning coal both add CO2 to the air.
post:
Post Lesson: Evolution and Ecosystems

Summary of Key Points

  • Natural selection needs four conditions: variation, inheritance, overproduction, and selection (Very Interesting Organisms Survive). Individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.
  • Populations evolve over generations; individuals do not. Acquired traits are not inherited.
  • Evidence for evolution: fossils, homologous structures, vestigial structures, similar embryos, and DNA and protein comparisons (fewer differences means a more recent common ancestor).
  • Food chain arrows point toward the eater, the direction energy flows. Producers → primary consumers → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers. Decomposers recycle nutrients from every level.
  • About 10% of the energy passes from one trophic level to the next. Going up, multiply by 0.10; going down, multiply by 10.
  • Energy flows; matter cycles. Photosynthesis removes CO2; respiration, decomposition, and burning add it. Bacteria fix nitrogen gas into forms plants can use and also return it to the air.

Exit Ticket

1. Name the four conditions of natural selection.

Show answer

Variation, inheritance, overproduction, and selection (differential survival and reproduction).

2. Producers capture 12,000 kcal. How much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?

Show answer

12,000 × 0.10 = 1,200 (primary); 1,200 × 0.10 = 120 (secondary); 120 × 0.10 = 12 kcal (tertiary).

3. In a food chain, does the arrow point toward the predator or toward the prey? Why?

Show answer

Toward the predator (the eater), because the arrow shows the direction energy moves.

4. Name two processes that return carbon dioxide to the air.

Show answer

Any two: cellular respiration, decomposition, burning fuels (combustion), volcanic eruptions.

5. Why do farmers sometimes plant beans or clover in a field before planting corn?

Show answer

Bacteria in the roots of beans and clover fix nitrogen, adding usable nitrogen to the soil for the next crop.

Reflection

  • Before this lesson, how would you have explained why insects become resistant to a pesticide? How would you explain it now?
  • Trace the energy in one meal you ate this week back to the sun. How many trophic levels did it pass through?
  • Which idea do you still mix up: arrow direction, the 10% rule, or which processes add or remove carbon dioxide? Write one sentence that will help you remember it.

This Week's Study Plan (20–40 minutes a day)

DayTask
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Make a card with “Very Interesting Organisms Survive” and “× 0.10 up, × 10 down.” Redo the five Try It problems without looking. (25 min)
Day 2Complete practice items 1–6. For each one you miss, read the explanation and write one sentence about why the correct answer is right. (30 min)
Day 3Complete practice items 7–12. Study the vocabulary list until you can define each term from memory. (30 min)
Day 4Draw a food web for a place you know (a park, a pond, your yard) with at least six organisms. Label producers, consumers, and decomposers. Make up an energy pyramid for it starting with 10,000 kcal. Review the Study Notes. (30 min)
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED Science test under timed conditions. (90 min, may be split over two days)
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Sort your mistakes by type (data reading, calculations, vocabulary) and reread that part of the lesson. (30–40 min)

Test-Taking Strategy: Check the Direction First

Before you answer any question about a population table, food web, or cycle, decide the direction: Is the trait going up or down over time? Which way do the arrows point? Is the process adding or removing something? Write a quick arrow (↑, ↓, or →) on your scratch paper. Many wrong answer choices on the GED are built by reversing the direction, so this ten-second check eliminates them quickly.

vocab.def: A change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations.
vocab.example: Over 50 years, the average beak size in a bird population increased.

vocab.def: The process in which individuals with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.
vocab.example: Dark lizards on dark rock are seen by birds less often, so more of them survive to have young.

vocab.def: An inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
vocab.example: A cactus's thick, waxy skin helps it hold water in the desert.

vocab.def: Differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
vocab.example: Some rabbits in a litter have thicker fur than others.

vocab.def: How well an organism survives and reproduces compared with others; measured by surviving offspring, not strength.
vocab.example: A small, well-hidden moth that has many offspring has high fitness.

vocab.def: An earlier species from which two or more later species are descended.
vocab.example: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago.

vocab.def: Body parts in different species that have the same basic structure but may have different functions, suggesting a common ancestor.
vocab.example: A human arm, a bat wing, and a whale flipper have the same arrangement of bones.

vocab.def: A body part that is reduced and has little or no use in an organism today but was useful in its ancestors.
An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms; primary consumers eat producers, secondary consumers eat primary consumers, and so on.
vocab.example: A rabbit (primary) eating grass; a fox (secondary) eating the rabbit.

vocab.def: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and wastes and returns nutrients to the soil.
vocab.example: Mushrooms and bacteria breaking down a fallen log.

vocab.def: A diagram of many connected food chains in an ecosystem, with arrows pointing from the food to the eater.
vocab.example: A pond web linking algae, snails, insects, fish, frogs, and herons.

vocab.example: Grass is level 1; a grasshopper is level 2; a frog that eats the grasshopper is level 3.

vocab.example: 10,000 kcal in plants → 1,000 kcal in rabbits → 100 kcal in foxes.

vocab.def: The changing of nitrogen gas from the air into a form living things can use, done mostly by bacteria.
vocab.example: Bacteria in the root bumps (nodules) of bean plants make ammonia from nitrogen gas.

notes:
Study Notes: Evolution and Ecosystems

Natural Selection: VIOS

Very Interesting Organisms Survive

  • Variation — individuals differ.
  • Inheritance — traits pass to offspring.
  • Overproduction — too many offspring; competition.
  • Selection — better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more.

Populations evolve, not individuals. Acquired traits are not inherited. The trait must exist before the change.

Evidence for Evolution

  • Fossils (older layers, transitional forms)
  • Homologous structures (same bones, different jobs)
  • Vestigial structures (tailbone)
  • Similar embryos
  • DNA/protein: fewer differences = closer relatives

Food Chains and Webs

Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary consumer. Arrow points to the eater (energy flow). Decomposers recycle every level.

10% Rule

Up one level: × 0.10. Down one level: × 10.
Actual % = (higher level ÷ lower level) × 100.
90% is used for life processes and lost as heat.

Cycles

Carbon: photosynthesis and oceans remove CO2; respiration, decomposition, burning, and volcanoes add CO2.
Nitrogen: fixation (N2 → ammonia, by bacteria/lightning) → nitrification (→ nitrates) → plants absorb → decomposers return ammonia → denitrification (→ N2).

LevelExampleEnergy (start 10,000 kcal)
1 ProducerGrass10,000
2 Primary consumerGrasshopper1,000
3 Secondary consumerFrog100
4 Tertiary consumerSnake10

Remember: energy flows one way; matter cycles. Remove a predator → prey rises → prey's food falls.

stimuli.title: Lizard Coloring After a Lava Flow
stimuli.html:
A small lizard species lives on a volcanic island. Before 2010, most of the island's ground was pale sand, and most of the lizards were light tan. A few lizards were dark brown. Biologists know that skin color in this species is inherited: dark parents usually have dark offspring, and light parents usually have light offspring. Hawks and gulls hunt the lizards by sight.

In 2010, a lava flow covered most of the pale sand with dark rock. Biologists counted the lizards in the same study area every two years. Each lizard lives about 2 to 3 years.

stimuli.title: Seasonal Carbon Dioxide Levels
stimuli.html: A monitoring station in the Northern Hemisphere measures the concentration of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the air. The graph shows the monthly average for one recent year, in parts per million (ppm). In the Northern Hemisphere, most trees and other plants grow leaves in spring and summer and lose them or stop growing in fall and winter.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the trend in the lizard population from 2010 to 2020?
options: The number of dark lizards increased while the number of light lizards decreased.
The numbers of both light and dark lizards increased.
The number of light lizards increased while the number of dark lizards decreased.
The total number of lizards dropped to about half of its 2010 size.
items.hint: Read each column from top to bottom. Which column goes up, and which goes down?
items.explain:
Dark lizards went from 120 (2010) to 450 (2020), an increase. Light lizards went from 480 to 150, a decrease. So dark increased while light decreased.

The reversed statement (light increased, dark decreased) is the most common error from reading the columns in the wrong order. The total did not drop by half: it stayed between 560 and 600 the whole time and was 600 in both 2010 and 2020.

items.prompt: Based on the food web, which organism is only a primary consumer?
options: Rabbit
Grass
Frog
Snake
items.hint: A primary consumer eats producers. Find an animal whose only food is a producer.
items.explain:
A primary consumer eats producers. The rabbit eats only grass, which is a producer, so the rabbit is a primary consumer.

Grass is a producer, not a consumer. The frog eats grasshoppers (primary consumers), so the frog is a secondary consumer. The snake eats mice and frogs, so it is a secondary or tertiary consumer, depending on the chain.

items.prompt: Each statement describes one condition of natural selection in the lizard population. Drag each statement to the condition it describes.
choices: Some lizards in the population are light tan and some are dark brown.
Dark parents usually have dark offspring.
Each female lays more eggs than can possibly survive to adulthood.
On the dark rock, hawks catch more light lizards than dark lizards.
items.hint: Variation = differences. Inheritance = passed to offspring. Overproduction = too many young. Selection = some survive better than others.
items.explain:
• Variation: lizards differ in color (light tan or dark brown).
  • Inheritance: color passes from parents to offspring.
  • Overproduction: more eggs are laid than can survive, so not every lizard can make it.
  • Selection: on dark rock, light lizards are easier for predators to see, so dark lizards survive and reproduce more.

A common mix-up is putting the predator statement under Variation. The predator statement is not about differences between lizards; it is about which lizards survive, which is selection.

items.prompt: What percentage of the lizards counted in 2020 were dark?
items.hint: Divide the number of dark lizards in 2020 by the total for 2020, then multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Dark lizards in 2020 = 450. Total in 2020 = 600.

450 ÷ 600 = 0.75

0.75 × 100 = 75%

A common error is dividing by the number of light lizards (450 ÷ 150 = 3, or 300%). The percentage of a population always uses the total as the denominator. For comparison, dark lizards were 120 ÷ 600 = 20% of the population in 2010.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the lizard population between 2010 and 2020?
options: Dark lizards were harder for hawks and gulls to see on the dark rock, so more of them survived and reproduced, passing dark coloring to their offspring.
Light lizards gradually changed to a dark color during their lives so that they would blend in with the new rock.
Chemicals from the lava caused mutations that turned light lizards dark in response to the new environment.
The total population grew rapidly after the lava flow, so there was enough food for more dark lizards to survive.
items.hint: Use the four conditions. Which lizards were more likely to survive long enough to have offspring?
items.explain:
This is natural selection. Dark coloring already existed (variation) and is inherited. On dark rock, predators that hunt by sight spotted light lizards more easily, so dark lizards survived and reproduced more. Over several generations (each lizard lives only 2 to 3 years), dark lizards became a larger share of the population.

The idea that light lizards changed color during their lives describes an acquired change in individuals; individuals do not evolve, and the passage says color is inherited. Mutations are random and are not produced on demand by the environment; the dark lizards were present before the lava flow. The population did not grow rapidly; the total stayed between 560 and 600.

items.prompt:
One food chain in this web is: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk.

items.hint: Count the steps: grass is the producer, and the grasshopper eats the grass. Read each arrow as “is eaten by.”
items.explain:
Blank 1: Grass is the producer, the grasshopper is the primary consumer, and the frog, which eats the grasshopper, is the secondary consumer.

Blank 2: Arrows show the direction energy flows, from the food to the eater, so they point to the organism that receives the energy. Choosing “is eaten” reverses the arrow.

Blank 3: Fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and wastes, so they are decomposers.

items.prompt: A disease kills most of the frogs in this grassland. Which change would most likely happen first?
options: The grasshopper population would increase, because fewer frogs would be eating grasshoppers.
The grass population would increase, because more grasshoppers would survive.
The snake population would increase, because snakes would have less competition for food.
The mouse population would decrease, because mice depend on frogs for food.
items.hint: Find what the frog eats. If its predator disappears, what happens to that prey?
items.explain:
According to the table, frogs eat grasshoppers. With most frogs gone, fewer grasshoppers are eaten, so the grasshopper population would most likely increase. This is the most direct, first effect.

The grass would not increase; more grasshoppers would eat more grass, so grass would likely decrease. Snakes eat frogs, so losing frogs takes away part of the snakes' food; snakes would not increase. Mice do not eat frogs (they eat grass seeds and grasshoppers), so the reason given for the mouse choice is false.

items.prompt: Read the description of the nitrogen cycle. Click the sentence that describes nitrogen fixation.
spans: Nitrogen gas makes up about 78 percent of the air, but most living things cannot use nitrogen in this form.
Bacteria living in small bumps on the roots of bean and clover plants change nitrogen gas into ammonia.
Other soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates.
Plants absorb nitrates through their roots and use the nitrogen to build proteins.
When plants and animals die, decomposers break down their remains and release ammonia into the soil.
Bacteria in waterlogged soil change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.
items.hint: Nitrogen fixation turns nitrogen gas from the air into a form living things can use.
items.explain:
Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of nitrogen gas (N2) into a usable form such as ammonia. The sentence about bacteria in bean and clover root bumps (nodules) changing nitrogen gas into ammonia describes exactly that.

The other sentences describe other steps: ammonia to nitrates is nitrification; plants absorbing nitrates is assimilation; decomposers releasing ammonia is ammonification; and nitrates changing back to nitrogen gas is denitrification, the reverse of fixation. The first sentence gives background but describes no process.

items.prompt: The producers in a meadow capture 30,000 kcal of energy per square meter per year. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?
items.hint: Go up two levels: producers to primary consumers, then primary to secondary. Multiply by 0.10 each time.
items.explain:
Producers: 30,000 kcal

Primary consumers: 30,000 × 0.10 = 3,000 kcal

Secondary consumers: 3,000 × 0.10 = 300 kcal

A common error is stopping after one step (3,000 kcal), which is the energy for primary consumers. Another is subtracting 10% at each step (30,000 − 3,000 = 27,000, then 27,000 − 2,700 = 24,300). The rule says only about 10% is passed on.

items.prompt: Between which two trophic levels was the percentage of energy transferred the greatest?
options: From primary consumers to secondary consumers
From producers to primary consumers
From secondary consumers to tertiary consumers
The percentage was exactly 10% between every pair of levels.
items.hint: For each step, divide the higher level's energy by the level below it and multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Calculate each transfer percentage:

Producers → primary: 1,200 ÷ 15,000 = 0.08 = 8%

Primary → secondary: 150 ÷ 1,200 = 0.125 = 12.5%

Secondary → tertiary: 12 ÷ 150 = 0.08 = 8%

The greatest percentage, 12.5%, is from primary consumers to secondary consumers.

The producers-to-primary step moved the greatest amount of energy (1,200 kcal), but the question asks for the greatest percentage, and that step was only 8%. The 10% rule is an approximation; real measurements vary, as these data show.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the CO2 level falls from May to September?
options: Plants in the Northern Hemisphere are growing and remove large amounts of CO<sub>2</sub> from the air through photosynthesis.
People burn more fossil fuels in summer, and burning removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air.
Animals stop cellular respiration during the warm months, so they release no CO<sub>2</sub>.
Decomposers break down more dead leaves in summer, which takes CO<sub>2</sub> out of the air.
items.hint: Which carbon cycle process removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the air, and when is it strongest in the Northern Hemisphere?
items.explain:
From May to September, the level drops from 424.0 ppm to 418.0 ppm, a decrease of 424.0 − 418.0 = 6.0 ppm. This is the Northern Hemisphere growing season. Leafy plants carry out a great deal of photosynthesis, which takes CO2 out of the air faster than respiration and other processes put it back. In fall and winter, photosynthesis slows while respiration and decomposition continue, so CO2 rises again.

Burning fossil fuels adds CO2; it does not remove it. Animals never stop cellular respiration while alive. Decomposition releases CO2 to the air; it does not remove it.

items.prompt:
Scientists compared the amino acid sequence of one protein in humans with the same protein in five other animals. The table shows the number of amino acid differences from the human version. (Values are for a classroom example.)

AnimalDifferences from human protein
Chimpanzee1
Mouse9
Chicken14
Frog19
Fish24

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Humans and mice share a more recent common ancestor than humans and frogs do.
Humans evolved directly from chimpanzees.
Of the animals listed, fish are the most closely related to humans.
Chickens and frogs are more closely related to each other than either is to humans.
items.hint: Fewer differences in a protein means two species are more closely related, sharing a more recent common ancestor.
items.explain:
Fewer amino acid differences indicate a closer relationship. The mouse protein has 9 differences from the human protein and the frog protein has 19. Since 9 < 19, humans are more closely related to mice, so humans and mice share a more recent common ancestor than humans and frogs do.

Only 1 difference with chimpanzees shows a very recent common ancestor, not that humans came from today's chimpanzees; both species descended from an earlier ancestor. Fish have the most differences (24), so they are the least closely related on the list. The table compares each animal only with humans, so it gives no information about how chickens and frogs compare with each other.
